forces: Two four-part choirs and two orchestras, with a soprano ripieno choir
performers: Münchener Bach-Chor and Münchener Chorknaben; Münchener Bach-Orchester; Karl Richter, conductor
question: How does Bach layer a dialogue between two choirs and a hymn over one steady pulse?
intro: This is the opening chorus of the St Matthew Passion, one of two selected highlights on this site and taken from a complete 1958 recording; the Passion has many further numbers. Two choirs and two orchestras call and answer while a boys’ choir sings a hymn above them.

cues.title: Two orchestras, one pulse
cues.text: The Passion opens in E minor and 12/8: four beats, each divided into three. Two identical orchestras play at once, each with two flutes, two oboes, violins, viola and continuo. For sixteen bars no one sings.
cues.evidence: The Bach-Gesellschaft score (IMSLP 00934), printed pp. 1–4, marks the double staves Coro I. II., sets the metre as 12/8 with one sharp and keeps the voice staves empty until the entry on p. 4. Wikipedia’s account of the movement also counts sixteen bars of instrumental introduction.

cues.title: The bass leaves its pedal
cues.text: For about half a minute the bass keeps returning to E, the tonic. Near 0:35 it moves to G and then to B, the dominant, and the rocking figures above begin to lean that way. Listen for the floor shifting beneath them.
cues.evidence: The report finds the bass on E in every window from 0:00 to 0:30, on G at 0:35 and on B from 0:40. Its boundaries in this stretch fall at 0:36 (0.55) and 0:44 (0.42), and the local-key estimate sits on B minor from 0:45 to 1:25. The key labels are estimates, not chord identifications.

cues.title: Words by Picander
cues.text: Christian Friedrich Henrici, who wrote as Picander, supplied the new poetry for this chorus, the arias and the closing chorus. The chorales and the Gospel narration were older. The Netherlands Bach Society says Picander probably worked in close consultation with Bach.
cues.evidence: Netherlands Bach Society, St Matthew Passion: https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-244. The Deutsche Grammophon booklet in the Internet Archive item credits Picander’s 1729 Leipzig poems as the source of the madrigal texts.

cues.title: Sixteen bars, then voices
cues.text: By the score’s proportions the first choir arrives about 1:45, after sixteen of the movement’s ninety bars. In this recording the level climbs by roughly ten decibels between 1:35 and 1:50 as the voices join, while the continuo’s lilting bass carries on beneath them.
cues.evidence: The choir enters in bar 17 of a ninety-bar movement (Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 4; the bars were counted from the printed pages and agree with Wikipedia’s sixteen-bar introduction), and 16/90 of 9:49 is about 1:45. Report: −20.5 dB at 1:35, −15.5 at 1:40, −12.2 at 1:45, −10.6 at 1:50; boundary at 1:48.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first choir alone
cues.text: The first choir sings ‘Kommt, ihr Töchter, helft mir klagen’ in four parts. The second choir’s singers rest, though its orchestra keeps playing. The recorded level stays high through this stretch, between about −10 and −7 dB, until near 2:30.
cues.evidence: In the Bach-Gesellschaft score (pp. 4–5) the second choir’s vocal staves are empty until the question ‘Wen?’ in bar 26 (p. 6), which Wikipedia also places in bar 26. Report: −10.6 dB at 1:50 and −7.0 dB at 2:25; the 2:25 window is among the five loudest. The singers’ entry is not aligned to a bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Whom? The bridegroom
cues.text: Around 2:45 the one-word questions begin. The first choir calls ‘Sehet’ — look — the second asks ‘Wen?’, and the answer is ‘den Bräutigam’, the bridegroom. In this recording the level eases by about five decibels as the exchange starts.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia places ‘Sehet’ and ‘Wen?’ in bar 26; with a sixteen-bar introduction and the entry at about 1:45, bar 26 falls near 2:40–2:45 by proportion. Report: −10.7 dB at 2:40, −13.0 at 2:45, −13.4 at 2:50, −15.2 at 2:55. The bar is not aligned to the audio.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The chorale above both choirs
cues.text: From bar 30, at about 3:05–3:10, the ripieno sopranos — a boys’ choir in this recording — sing ‘O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig’ above the choirs, while the first choir restates ‘Kommt, ihr Töchter’ beneath. The level rises from 3:10 to 3:25, the loudest window of the track.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia: the cantus firmus starts in bar 30. The score has a separate Soprano ripieno staff, and the Deutsche Grammophon booklet assigns the chorale to the Knabenchor. Report: −13.2 dB at 3:10, −9.9 at 3:15, −6.9 at 3:20, −5.3 at 3:25; the 3:25 window is the loudest of the track.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Follow the top line
cues.text: Follow the highest line: the chorale is sung in sustained notes, one phrase at a time, while the choirs below trade short exchanges. Bach’s Leipzig listeners knew this hymn, so its plea would have been recognisable even as the choirs interrupt one another.
cues.evidence: A listening suggestion drawn from the score’s separate ripieno staff. The recording cannot separate the boys’ voices from the choirs, so no timing beyond the entry near 3:08 is claimed. The Netherlands Bach Society notes that the chorale texts and melodies were familiar to the congregation.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The choirs rest, then return
cues.text: At about 4:05 the level falls by roughly ten decibels and stays low for half a minute: in the score the main choirs pause for a few bars. Near 4:35 it jumps back as they return with ‘Sehet … seht die Geduld’ — see the patience — and the question ‘Was?’
cues.evidence: Report: −11.0 dB at 4:00, −17.6 at 4:05, −21.3 at 4:20 and 4:30, then −12.8 at 4:35 (boundary 0.82 at 4:36; a smaller one at 4:24). The Bach-Gesellschaft score (p. 10) shows the choir staves silent for several bars before ‘Sehet, seht die Ge-’; Wikipedia lists the Sehet — Was? — seht die Geduld exchange. Score timing is approximate.

cues.title: A Lutheran Agnus Dei
cues.text: ‘O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig’ is Nikolaus Decius’s German paraphrase of the Agnus Dei, published in 1531. The Netherlands Bach Society notes that the chorale texts and melodies in the Passion came from the hymn book and were familiar to the Leipzig congregation.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia, ‘O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig’ (published 1531, based on the Agnus Dei); the Deutsche Grammophon booklet names Decius as the chorale’s author for No. 1; Netherlands Bach Society, https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-244.

cues.title: Short questions, long answers
cues.text: From here to about 7:00 the second choir’s questions — ‘Was?’ and then ‘Wohin?’, where to? — interrupt the first choir’s longer replies. Listen for how quickly each question is put and how the answer, ‘auf unsre Schuld’ — on our guilt — settles it.
cues.evidence: The exchanges Sehet — Was? — seht die Geduld and Seht — Wohin? — auf unsre Schuld are listed in Wikipedia’s account and in the Netherlands Bach Society text. Their positions here are inferred from the score’s proportions and the report’s level changes, not aligned to bars.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The texture lightens
cues.text: From about 5:40 the level drops by some ten decibels for roughly half a minute, and the sound becomes brighter. The report cannot say which voices or instruments thin out; the score is in the middle of its question-and-answer stretch.
cues.evidence: Report: −10.3 dB at 5:30, −17.0 at 5:35, −21.8 at 5:40 and −17.9 to −20.9 through 6:10; brightness about 1,500 Hz before and 1,950–2,030 Hz at 5:50–6:05; boundary 0.51 at 5:40. No instrument or voice is identified.

cues.title: A sudden hush
cues.text: The strongest boundary of the movement falls at 6:16. Within seconds the level drops by about ten decibels and stays low for some fifteen seconds, among the quietest stretches of the track. By proportion the score is near the question ‘Wohin?’, though the cause of the thin sound is not measured.
cues.evidence: Report: boundary strength 1.00 at 6:16 (0.87 at 6:20, 0.64 at 6:32); −13.6 dB at 6:15, −23.2 at 6:20, −24.8 at 6:25, −14.6 at 6:30; 6:20 and 6:25 are two of the five quietest windows. The link to ‘Wohin?’ comes from score proportion only.

cues.title: Good Friday vespers
cues.text: In Leipzig the Passion belonged to Good Friday vespers and was performed in two parts, one before the sermon and one after. This chorus opens the first part. Scholars usually place the first performance in 1727, although older sources say 1729.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia, St Matthew Passion: two parts performed before and after the sermon, and the usual dating to Good Friday 1727 since 1975 with 1729 as the older date. The Netherlands Bach Society gives the occasion as vespers on Good Friday in the Thomaskirche and dates the first performance between 1725 and 1728 or to 1729.

cues.title: The poem’s last lines
cues.text: Near 7:15 the level rises by about six decibels as the choirs sing the poem’s last lines in separate blocks: ‘Sehet ihn aus Lieb und Huld Holz zum Kreuze selber tragen’ — see him carry the cross’s wood himself, out of love and grace. The chorale’s last line is ‘Erbarm dich unser’.
cues.evidence: Report: −17.0 dB at 7:05, −14.1 at 7:10, −7.8 at 7:15 (boundary 0.80 at 7:14); 6:55 is the second-quietest window. Wikipedia says Chorus I and II sing the last lines of the text in separate blocks; the Netherlands Bach Society text places ‘Erbarm dich unser, o Jesu’ as the chorale’s final line.

cues.title: Bach in Leipzig
cues.text: Bach had been Thomaskantor in Leipzig since 1723 and had given the city his St John Passion in 1724. The St Matthew Passion followed, in a revised form in 1736 that survives in an autograph score now in Berlin (Mus. ms. Bach P 25).
cues.evidence: Bach’s appointment in 1723 and the St John Passion of 1724: this site’s Bach biography. The 1736 revision: Netherlands Bach Society. The manuscript, Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin Mus. ms. Bach P 25, is catalogued on IMSLP’s St Matthew Passion page.

cues.title: Mendelssohn, 1829
cues.text: In 1829 Felix Mendelssohn conducted an abridged St Matthew Passion in Berlin, a landmark in the nineteenth-century revival of Bach’s large choral works. Karl Richter recorded the whole Passion in Munich in 1958, in 22 sessions; Archiv issued it on four stereo LPs.
cues.evidence: Mendelssohn’s abridged performance in Berlin in 1829: this site’s Bach biography. The 22 sessions between 23 June and 21 August 1958 and the stereo technique: the Deutsche Grammophon booklet in the Internet Archive item. The first complete recording on disc, made in the Herkulessaal for Archiv Produktion in July and August 1958: the Karl Richter chronicle at karlrichtermunich.blogspot.com. The four-LP stereo set, SAPM 198 009/012: Discogs and Wikipedia.

cues.title: The opening words return
cues.text: About 8:40, after the chorale has ended, the choirs sing the poem’s first lines again, ‘Kommt, ihr Töchter, helft mir klagen’. Only about nine bars remain. In this recording the estimated harmony rests on B for about forty seconds before turning to E.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia: the first lines return from bar 82 to the end in bar 90, after the cantus firmus has died out. By proportion bar 82 falls between about 8:35 and 8:50. Report: local-key estimates B minor from 8:35 to 9:05, B major at 9:10–9:15, E minor from 9:20. The return is not aligned to a bar.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The dominant, then home
cues.text: At about 9:10–9:15 the estimates show B major, the dominant. By 9:20 they have turned to E minor, the key of the opening, and the level stays high, near −10 dB, to the final bars. Listen for the arrival of the cadence rather than one chord.
cues.evidence: Report: B major (r 0.58) at 9:10 and (0.53) at 9:15; E minor (0.59) at 9:20, (0.68) at 9:25, (0.62) at 9:30 and (0.59) at 9:35; level −10.1, −10.9, −12.3 and −10.7 dB over those windows. The estimates confirm a return to E but identify no chord.

cues.title: The last chord
cues.text: The final sustained chord begins about 9:38 and fades by the end of the file, with E in the bass. On the full recording the Evangelist’s first recitative follows; this selection does not include it.
cues.evidence: Report: onset rate 1.6 per second at 9:35, 0.6 at 9:40 and 0.4 at 9:45; level −8.8 dB at 9:40 and −21.5 at 9:45; bass E and local key E at 9:40–9:45. The Internet Archive item lists the Evangelist’s recitative ‘Da Jesus diese Rede vollendet hatte’ as the next track.

transitions.title: Voices join a pulse already moving
transitions.how: The introduction’s swaying 12/8 figures do not stop for the voices. The continuo’s lilting, repeated-note bass carries on beneath the first choir, which enters in the seventeenth bar on ‘Kommt, ihr Töchter, helft mir klagen’, singing in four parts while both orchestras keep playing. The join adds voices to a texture already in motion instead of starting a new section: the same E-minor pulse now carries words, and the second choir has not yet spoken.
transitions.evidence: The entry is in bar 17 of 90 (Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 4; Wikipedia counts sixteen bars of introduction), which by proportion is about 1:45. Report: relative level −20.5 dB at 1:35 rising to −10.6 dB at 1:50; boundary 0.40 at 1:48. The continuing bass pattern is read from the printed continuo staff, not separated in the audio.

transitions.title: A hymn is laid over the dialogue
transitions.how: At bar 30 the ripieno sopranos enter with the first line of ‘O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig’, a hymn tune sung in sustained notes above music that has been moving in short question-and-answer phrases. The first choir restates its opening text beneath the hymn and the questions continue, so the join is a layering, not a cadence: a third strand is added at the top while the two choirs keep their dialogue below. The score gives the ripieno its own staff, marked Soprano ripieno.
transitions.evidence: Wikipedia places the cantus firmus entry in bar 30; the Bach-Gesellschaft score has a separate Soprano ripieno staff and the Deutsche Grammophon booklet gives the chorale to the boys’ choir. By proportion bar 30 is about 3:05–3:10. Report: level −13.2 dB at 3:10 rising to −5.3 dB at 3:25, the loudest window of the track.

transitions.title: Single-word questions give way to blocks
transitions.to: C · Last lines of the poem
transitions.how: The questions ‘Wen?’, ‘Wie?’, ‘Was?’ and ‘Wohin?’ have all been asked. After the last answer, ‘auf unsre Schuld’ (on our guilt), the two choirs stop trading single words and sing the poem’s final lines in separate blocks: ‘Sehet ihn aus Lieb und Huld Holz zum Kreuze selber tragen’ — see him carry the wood of the cross himself, out of love and grace. In this recording the level reaches one of its quietest windows near 6:55 and then rises by about six decibels.
transitions.evidence: Wikipedia and the Netherlands Bach Society text list the questions, the answer ‘auf unsre Schuld’ and the final lines sung in blocks. Report: 6:55 is the second-quietest window (−25.6 dB); −17.0 dB at 7:05, −14.1 at 7:10, −7.8 at 7:15; boundary 0.80 at 7:14. The bar of the change is not aligned.

transitions.title: The first words come back, then home
transitions.from: C · Last lines of the poem
transitions.how: Once the chorale has ended, the choirs return to the first lines of the poem, ‘Kommt, ihr Töchter, helft mir klagen’, from bar 82; only about nine bars remain. Before the close, the estimated harmony stays on B, the dominant, for some forty seconds of the recording, then turns to E from about 9:20. The movement ends on a sustained E, so the opening’s tonic is restored after a long span that never settled on it.
transitions.evidence: Wikipedia: the first lines return from bar 82 to bar 90 after the cantus firmus has ended. Proportion places bar 82 between about 8:35 and 8:50. Report: B-minor estimates 8:35–9:05, B major at 9:10–9:15, E minor from 9:20, bass E at 9:40–9:45. These are estimates of key region, not identified chords.

source.title: Bach, Passionsmusik nach dem Evangelisten Matthäus (Matthäus-Passion), BWV 244, Bach-Gesellschaft Ausgabe, vol. 4, Erster Theil (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1854)
source.locator: No. 1, printed pp. 1–21 (PDF pp. 3–23): Coro I and Coro II each with two flutes, two oboes, violins I–II, viola, four voices and continuo, plus a Soprano ripieno staff. The recording’s booklet lists oboes d’amore and da caccia and a continuo of organ, cello, double bass and bassoon without assigning them to numbers, so the timeline shows the continuo as organ, cellos and basses. Entry times follow bar proportion (a 16-bar introduction of 90 bars) and the report’s level changes; they are approximate.

timeline.note: Both orchestras play the same rocking 12/8 figures over the continuo’s repeated-note bass; no voices yet.
The first choir enters on ‘Kommt, ihr Töchter’ above both orchestras; the second choir’s singers wait.
The second choir joins with its one-word questions (‘Wen?’, ‘Wie?’) and the first choir answers.
The ripieno sopranos add the chorale ‘O Lamm Gottes’ in sustained notes above both choirs.
After the choirs’ pause, the questions ‘Was?’ and ‘Wohin?’ alternate with the first choir’s answers while the chorale continues.
The choirs sing the poem’s last lines in separate blocks; the chorale reaches its final line.
The chorale has ended; the opening words return and the movement closes on a sustained E.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Münchener Bach-Chor (chorus (Chorus I and II)), Münchener Chorknaben (boys’ choir, ripieno soprano (chorale ‘O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig’)), Münchener Bach-Orchester (orchestra), Karl Richter (conductor)
fields.note: The booklet track list gives the chorale to the Knabenchor. The booklet also names instrumental soloists for the whole Passion (flutes Walther Theurer and Wolfgang Haag; oboes Edgar Shann and Kurt Hausmann; organ Ekkehard Tietze and Hedwig Bilgram; double bass Franz Ortner; bassoon Karl Kolbinger; viola da gamba Oswald Uhl), and Fritz Rothschuh as chorus master. Their assignment to this number is not stated, so they are not listed as performers of it.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition is not identified. The booklet gives the composition as Leipzig 1729 or earlier, revised 1736, and cites the autograph score Mus. ms. Bach P 25 and the parts St 110. The booklet and the Bach-Gesellschaft score number this chorus No. 1; the New Bach Edition also numbers it 1.

Which session produced No. 1 is not stated.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: territorial — European recording-rights expiry; first publication documented before 1963 (Archiv Produktion stereo LP edition, 1958 or 1959).
fields.note: Programme rule 3. The recording was made in June–August 1958 and first issued on four stereo LPs; the booklet states 1959 and quotes a critic’s review of the four LPs from May 1959. Whether the first issue fell in 1958 or 1959, a recording published by 1959 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term (to the end of 2009) before the extension that applied from 1 November 2013. This is territorial, not a licence: the Internet Archive item carries no licence URL and no Public Domain Mark. US status is not established and no US public-domain claim is made. The audio file is a later commercial digital remaster; this dossier relies on the first publication of the recording and does not separately clear any rights claimed in the remastering, which is a point for the integration lead.

composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players
Cantatas, Passions, the B minor Mass, organ and keyboard cycles, concertos, unaccompanied string music
composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.
